notes: Facts about Međugorje, Bosnia and Herzegovina, written neutrally. Distances, heights and visitor numbers are approximate. Add or edit entries freely: 'always' entries are always known; other entries are used when a keyword matches.

entries.title: Where Međugorje is
entries.text: Međugorje (also spelled Medjugorje) is a village in Herzegovina, in the south-west of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the municipality of Čitluk and the Herzegovina-Neretva Canton. It lies about 25–30 km south-west of Mostar, not far from the Croatian border, at roughly 43.2° N, 17.68° E. A few thousand people live there. It has been a major Catholic pilgrimage destination since 1981, when six young locals reported seeing the Virgin Mary.

entries.title: Where you are: Međugorje in general
entries.text: You are in Međugorje, a small village in Herzegovina, in the south-west of Bosnia and Herzegovina, about 25 km from Mostar and close to the Croatian border. It lies in a valley between two hills, Podbrdo (Apparition Hill) and Križevac (Cross Mountain). Since 1981, when six young people reported seeing Our Lady on Podbrdo, it has become one of the best-known Catholic pilgrimage places in the world, visited by about a million people a year. The centre of everything is St. James Church, with daily evening prayer, and around it are guesthouses, hotels, shops and restaurants. Visitors climb the two hills, go to Mass and confession, and enjoy the local wine and food.

entries.title: How to talk about faith topics
entries.text: The apparitions and the faith around them are sensitive topics. Speak respectfully and neutrally: say what believers report and what the Church has said, do not present miracles as proven fact, do not mock believers or sceptics, and do not pressure anyone. Visitors of all faiths and none are welcome in the village. If you are unsure about a detail, say so.

entries.title: Language, money and borders
entries.text: People in Međugorje speak Croatian (the Herzegovina region is mostly Croat), and in the pilgrim trade many also speak English, Italian, German, Polish and other languages. The currency of Bosnia and Herzegovina is the convertible mark (KM or BAM), tied to the euro, and euros are often accepted in village shops and restaurants. The time zone is Central European Time. Bosnia and Herzegovina is not in the EU, so travellers coming from Croatia cross a border and need a valid ID or passport.

entries.title: Getting to Međugorje
entries.text: From Mostar it is roughly 25–30 km by road. From Split, Dubrovnik or Sarajevo it takes about 2.5 hours by road, and the Split and Dubrovnik routes cross the Croatian–Bosnian border. Pilgrim groups usually fly into Dubrovnik, Split or Sarajevo. Buses and shuttles run from Mostar. During big events such as the Youth Festival, traffic in the village can be very heavy.

entries.title: History of the parish and the name
entries.text: The Catholic parish of St. James (Sveti Jakov) was founded in 1892 and has long been served by Franciscan friars. The name Međugorje is usually understood to mean 'between the mountains' (međ = between, gorje = mountains). The first parish church dated from 1897; after the First World War it became unsafe because of unstable ground. In 1933–34 the parishioners built a large concrete cross on Cross Mountain (Križevac) for the Holy Year marking 1,900 years since Christ's death. The present St. James Church was built in 1969.

entries.title: The first reported apparitions in 1981
entries.text: On 24 June 1981, two teenage girls, Ivanka Ivanković and Mirjana Dragićević, reported seeing a bright figure of a woman on Podbrdo hill above the village. The other four — Vicka Ivanković, Ivan Dragićević, Marija Pavlović and Jakov Čolo — joined them within the first two days. They were aged between about 10 and 17. They described a young woman with a crown of stars whom they called Gospa (Our Lady). The parish priest, Fr. Jozo Zovko, was at first sceptical and was later imprisoned by the communist authorities. The anniversary is marked on 25 June each year.

entries.title: The six visionaries
entries.text: The six people known as the visionaries are Marija Pavlović-Lunetti, Ivan Dragićević, Vicka Ivanković-Mijatović, Jakov Čolo, Mirjana Dragićević-Soldo and Ivanka Ivanković-Elez. They are now adults with families. According to reports, Mirjana shares a message on the 2nd of each month and a monthly message is published on the 25th (through Marija); some of them report apparitions only on particular dates, for example Ivanka on 25 June and Jakov at Christmas. Accounts differ in detail. The Vatican's 2024 note says the visionaries are no longer seen as the central figures of the Međugorje experience, and advises pilgrims to come for prayer and the sacraments rather than to meet them.

entries.title: What the Catholic Church says
entries.text: The Church's position has developed over time. In 1991 the bishops of Yugoslavia (the Zadar declaration) said that, on the basis of the investigations so far, it could not be affirmed that these were supernatural apparitions. A Vatican commission led by Cardinal Camillo Ruini studied the events from 2010 to 2014. In 2018 Pope Francis appointed Archbishop Henryk Hoser as his envoy for the pastoral care of pilgrims, and in May 2019 he authorised official pilgrimages without confirming the apparitions. On 19 September 2024 the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, with the Pope's approval, issued the note 'The Queen of Peace' granting a 'nihil obstat' (no objection): it recognises many positive spiritual fruits and allows public devotion, but does not declare the apparitions supernatural, and Catholics are not obliged to believe in them.

entries.title: Messages and the five stones
entries.text: The messages attributed to Our Lady of Međugorje, who is called the Queen of Peace, centre on peace, conversion, prayer, fasting, forgiveness and a closer relationship with Jesus. Priests in Međugorje often sum them up as five 'stones': daily prayer (especially the rosary), the Eucharist (Mass), reading the Bible, fasting (traditionally on Wednesdays and Fridays) and monthly confession. Many pilgrims say they come for quiet prayer, confession and a fresh start. The Vatican's 2024 note praises the emphasis on peace and a God-centred faith, while saying that not everything connected with such an experience is thereby endorsed.

entries.title: St. James Church
entries.text: St. James Church (Crkva sv. Jakova) is the parish church and the heart of the pilgrimage. It has two tall bell towers, holds more than two thousand people, and has an outdoor altar area for the evening Mass when the crowds are big. Many confessionals stand on the grounds so that priests can hear confessions in many languages. There is an Adoration chapel nearby, and behind the church a large statue of Christ rising from the cross, where pilgrims say drops of water appear on the knee. Evening prayer — the rosary, Mass and devotions — takes place every day, with the times shifting between summer and winter.

entries.title: Apparition Hill (Podbrdo)
entries.text: Podbrdo, known to pilgrims as Apparition Hill, is the rocky hill above the village where the first reported apparitions happened in 1981 (it is part of Mount Crnica). A stony path of about half an hour leads up, passing stations for the mysteries of the rosary, to a statue of Our Lady that marks the spot. A Blue Cross is another landmark on the hill. The stones are sharp and can be slippery, so sturdy shoes matter, and it gets very hot in summer. The path is free and open all day.

entries.title: Cross Mountain (Križevac)
entries.text: Križevac (Cross Mountain) rises west of the village, at around 520 m above sea level. At the top is a large concrete cross built by the parishioners in 1933–34 for the Holy Year of the Redemption, inspired by their pastor Fr. Bernardin Smoljan. The parish describes it as roughly 8.5 m high, although guidebooks quote different numbers. A path with 14 Stations of the Cross leads up and takes around 45 to 60 minutes, with rocky, slippery sections. The Exaltation of the Holy Cross is celebrated here on the first Sunday after 8 September.

entries.title: Mladifest, the Youth Festival
entries.text: Mladifest, the Međugorje International Youth Festival, takes place every year from 1 to 6 August. It began in 1989 and is organised by the Međugorje parish. Around 50,000 young people from many countries come for prayer, Mass, adoration, confession, talks, music and testimonies. It is the second-largest regular Catholic youth gathering after World Youth Day. Traffic and accommodation in the village are very busy during that week.

entries.title: How many people visit
entries.text: Estimates of the number of visitors vary. Catholic media often say more than 40 million pilgrims have come since 1981, and local guides talk about roughly a million visitors in a typical year, more in peak years. Pilgrimage and tourism are now the main source of income in the village, which has many guesthouses, hotels, shops and restaurants. Many visitors come from Italy, Poland, Ireland, the USA, Croatia and other countries.

entries.title: Communities and charity
entries.text: Around Međugorje there are several charitable and spiritual communities. Community Cenacolo, which helps young people recover from addiction, has a house there, and its members often give testimonies at the Youth Festival. Mother's Village (Majčino selo) is a home for children in need, set up around the parish. Many pilgrims also volunteer or donate to such projects.

entries.title: Who runs the parish
entries.text: The parish is served by Franciscan friars from the Herzegovina province. Church-wise, Međugorje belongs to the Diocese of Mostar-Duvno, whose bishop in 2024 was Petar Palić. Since 2018 the Pope has had a special envoy for the pastoral care of pilgrims; after Archbishop Hoser died in 2021, Bishop Aldo Cavalli took over that role.

entries.title: Mostar and the Old Bridge
entries.text: Mostar is the nearest big city, about 25–30 km away. Its Old Bridge (Stari Most), a graceful stone arch over the Neretva river, was destroyed in the 1993 war and rebuilt in 2004, and the old town is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Many visitors combine Međugorje with a day in Mostar.

entries.title: Other places to see nearby
entries.text: Close to Međugorje you can also visit the Kravice waterfalls, a wide curtain of falls on the Trebižat river near Ljubuški where people swim in summer; Počitelj, an Ottoman-era hillside fortress village near Čapljina; and Blagaj, with its old dervish house at the spring of the Buna river near Mostar. Each is a short drive, roughly 30 to 60 minutes.

entries.title: Food and wine
entries.text: Herzegovina has a strong food and wine tradition. Local wines come from the native grapes Žilavka (white) and Blatina (red), and there are family-run wineries around Čitluk. Typical foods include cured ham (pršut), local cheese, lamb and hearty stews. Restaurants in Međugorje mostly serve Croatian-Herzegovinian cooking.

entries.title: Landscape and weather
entries.text: The landscape is Mediterranean karst: pale limestone hills, vineyards and fields in the valleys, with vines and tobacco as traditional crops. Summers are hot and dry and the limestone reflects the heat, so early morning or late afternoon is best for climbing the hills. Winters are mild but can be rainy, with cool nights. The village sits in a valley between Podbrdo (on Mount Crnica) and Križevac.

entries.title: Etiquette for visitors
entries.text: The churches in Međugorje are active places of prayer. Visitors are asked to dress modestly (covered shoulders and knees), keep their voices down and be respectful with photos during prayer. Everyone is welcome, whatever they believe. Confessions are offered in many languages. Water and sturdy shoes are a good idea for the hills.

entries.title: Important dates
entries.text: Notable dates in Međugorje: 24–25 June, the anniversary of the first reported apparition in 1981; 1–6 August, the Youth Festival; the first Sunday after 8 September, the Exaltation of the Holy Cross on Križevac; Christmas and Easter, with large celebrations; and the 2nd and 25th of each month, when reported messages are shared and many pilgrims gather.

entries.title: A typical pilgrim's day
entries.text: A typical day for pilgrims: morning prayer or Mass, a climb up Apparition Hill or Cross Mountain, confession and quiet time, then the evening programme at St. James Church with the rosary, Mass and often adoration. Many pilgrims stay from a few days to a week, in family guesthouses and hotels close to the church.
